## Welcome & Course Aim

### Why this course

| Clinicians increasingly need to analyse their own data and read statistics critically.
| R is free, reproducible and the standard tool in modern clinical research.

### Our promise

| Start from zero - no programming background assumed.
| Learn by doing, using ONE real clinical dataset all week.
| Finish able to produce publication-ready tables, figures and regression results.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Learning by analogy
Think of R as a very precise research assistant: you write the instructions once, it repeats them perfectly forever.
:::

::: {.notes}
Set the tone: supportive, practical, clinically relevant.

Common misconception: 'I am not a maths/computer person so R is not for me.' Reframe: R is a skill like using a new clinical device - learnable with practice.

Clinical interpretation: reproducibility protects you in audits, revisions and re-analysis.

Audience question: how many currently use Excel/SPSS/Stata? Expected: most - bridge from there.

Demo tip: keep the first day light on jargon.
:::

## Who This Course Is For

[Designed for busy clinical professionals - no programming experience needed.]{.slide-intro}

- Medical doctors and residents
- Nurses and hospital research staff
- Clinical and hospital pharmacists
- Clinical researchers and trial coordinators
- Public health professionals
- Masters students and PhD candidates
- Anyone who collects or interprets clinical data

::: {.notes}
Establish the shared starting point.

Key teaching point: the mix of backgrounds is a strength - pair confident with less confident learners.

Common misconception: that statisticians and clinicians need different tools - they do not.

Audience question: what is your single biggest data frustration today? Expected: cleaning, or 'I cannot reproduce last year's analysis'.

Demo tip: note names/roles to tailor examples.
:::

## Learning Objectives (1 of 2)

### By the end of the week you will be able to

- Navigate R and RStudio with confidence.
- Understand the structure of clinical datasets.
- Import data from Excel and CSV files.
- Clean, validate and recode clinical data.
- Perform and interpret descriptive statistics.
- Generate publication-quality tables (a manuscript Table 1).
- Generate publication-quality figures.

::: {.notes}
Walk through objectives 1-7 (the data-handling and description skills).

Key teaching point: these map one-to-one onto the five days.

Clinical interpretation: each objective is a step in a real manuscript workflow.

Audience question: which objective matters most to you? Expected: varies - reassure all are covered.

Demo tip: return to this list at each day's recap to show progress.
:::

## Learning Objectives (2 of 2)

### You will also be able to

- Choose and perform common statistical tests.
- Interpret statistical output correctly.
- Perform simple and multiple logistic regression.
- Report odds ratios with confidence intervals.
- Write reproducible analysis scripts.
- Export publication-ready outputs.
- Interpret findings for medical publications.

::: {.notes}
Objectives 8-13 (the analysis, inference and reporting skills).

Key teaching point: interpretation is weighted as heavily as computation throughout.

Common misconception: that running the test is the hard part - interpreting and reporting it well is harder.

Audience question: who has had a paper criticised for statistics? Expected: a few - this course prevents that.

Demo tip: emphasise we always ask 'what does this mean clinically?'
:::

## Course Structure - Five Sessions

| Session | Theme | Core skill | Exercise output |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | Introduction to R & RStudio | Import data | Dataset imported |
| 2 | Understanding & Cleaning Clinical Data | Clean & recode | Analysis-ready data |
| 3 | Descriptive Statistics, Tables & Figures | Tables & figures | Manuscript Table 1 |
| 4 | Common Medical Statistical Tests | t-test, Chi-square, Non-parametric | Correct test chosen |
| 5 | Introduction to Regression & Interpreting Output | Modelling & reporting | Short Results section |

: Five evening sessions (Tuesdays, 90 minutes each); each session builds on the last.

::: {.notes}
Give the map of the whole week.

Key teaching point: skills are cumulative - Day 2's clean data feeds every later day.

Clinical interpretation: this is exactly how a real analysis project flows, start to finish.

Audience question: which day looks most daunting? Expected: Days 4-5 - reassure we build up gently.

Demo tip: keep this slide handy to re-orient anyone who feels lost.
:::

## How Each Session Runs (90 Minutes)

### A predictable evening rhythm

| Recap & set-up - about 10 minutes: reconnect to last week.
| Lecture & live demo - about 55 minutes: concepts, then the trainer codes as you watch.
| Guided exercise - about 20 minutes: you code, we help.
| Wrap-up & questions - throughout and in the last 5 minutes.

::: {.callout-note}
## Bring
A laptop with R and RStudio installed (see the pre-course pack), and the course data folder.
:::

::: {.notes}
Explain the format so participants know what to expect each session.

Key teaching point: watching then doing (the demo-then-exercise pattern) is how coding is learned.

Common mistake: trying to type along during the demo and falling behind - watch first, code in the exercise.

Audience question: prefer to type along or watch then do? Expected: mixed - explain why watch-first works.

Demo tip: share your screen with a large font (e.g. 16-18pt).
:::

## Our Case Study - One Dataset All Week

### Study

| Determinants of Hypertension Treatment Uptake among Adults attending Primary Healthcare Facilities.

### Design

| Multicentre cross-sectional study - 6 primary healthcare facilities.
| 1,500 adult attendees screened for hypertension.
| Facilities: Bugando PHC, Kisesa HC, Nyamagana PHC, Ilemela HC, Buzuruga PHC, Igoma HC.

### Primary outcome

| Treatment uptake - whether a diagnosed patient is currently on antihypertensive therapy.

::: {.notes}
Introduce the single dataset that anchors every exercise.

Key teaching point: using one realistic dataset all week lets skills compound.

Clinical interpretation: treatment uptake is a real implementation-science question - many diagnosed patients never start therapy.

Audience question: why might a diagnosed patient not be on treatment? Expected: cost, distance, beliefs, no insurance - these are our predictors.

Demo tip: this is simulated data built to behave realistically - safe to share and reproduce.
:::

## The Variables We Will Use

### Demographics & social

| Age, sex, residence, education, occupation, marital status, health insurance.

### Behavioural & clinical

| Smoking, alcohol, physical activity, BMI, diabetes, family history, blood pressure.

### Laboratory & outcomes

| Cholesterol panel, glucose, creatinine, electrolytes; treatment uptake, adherence, BP control.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Data dictionary
A full data dictionary (36 variables) is provided - keep it open during every exercise.
:::

::: {.notes}
Preview the data dictionary so variables are familiar before Day 1's import.

Key teaching point: knowing your variables and their types is half of good analysis.

Common misconception: more variables is always better - we will discuss parsimony on Day 5.

Clinical interpretation: these span the determinants framework (predisposing, enabling, need factors).

Audience question: which variable would you expect to predict uptake? Expected: insurance, diabetes, education - we will test this.

Demo tip: hand out the printed data dictionary now.
:::

## How the Week Builds to a Published Result

### The analysis pipeline

| Import (Day 1)  -\>  Clean & validate (Day 2)  -\>  Describe (Day 3)
| Test & model (Day 4)  -\>  Final model, interpret & report (Day 5).

### Your final deliverable

| A short, reproducible Results section identifying the determinants of treatment uptake -
| exactly what a journal would expect.

::: {.callout-note}
## The big idea
Every day produces one piece of a real manuscript; by Friday the pieces form a whole analysis.
:::

::: {.notes}
Show the throughline so participants see the destination from Day 1.

Key teaching point: analysis is a pipeline, not a single magic command.

Clinical interpretation: reproducibility means a reviewer could rerun your script and get your numbers.

Audience question: where do most analyses go wrong? Expected: cleaning and interpretation - hence two full sessions on them.

Demo tip: revisit this pipeline diagram at each session's start.
:::
